## Probable Cause
A reasonable belief, supported by evidence or testimony, that a specific individual [bold]has committed, is committing, or intends to commit[/bold] a crime.
Probable cause is the [bold]threshold for arrest and warrants[/bold]. It requires more than suspicion — it must be grounded in articulable, specific facts.
### What Probable Cause Permits
- Arrest and detention - Application for and execution of search warrants - Personal searches incident to arrest - Seizure of evidence - Implant searches where otherwise authorized by law
### How Probable Cause May Be Established
- Direct observation of a crime being committed - Physical evidence linking the individual to a crime - Security records (camera footage, access logs, station records) - Forensic evidence - Credible witness testimony - Admissions or confessions
Probable cause does [bold]not[/bold] require absolute certainty, but must be supported by facts an officer can clearly articulate — not a hunch.
[bold][color=#ffffff]Example[/color][/bold]
During lawful investigatory detention, the officer questions the Research Assistant seen circling the bridge. The individual then flees. The officer gives a clear order to stop, and the individual continues fleeing. This establishes probable cause for [textlink="119 — Resist, Delay, or Obstruct Justice" link="HLSpaceLawList"]. Security uses a disabler to stop the individual, applies restraints, and conducts a search incident to arrest. During that lawful search, Security finds an access breaker and a syndicate uplink. Security has now lawfully located and arrested a syndicate operative before they could cause harm.
